proves: Rule 1. A caller's overlay outranks a governed pin: the catalog pins ID to Identifier and the answer is Identity, tagged custom so nobody mistakes it for the standard. entry_id is null because a bare string overlay has no row to cite.
The same token with no overlay, so the contrast above is a change the overlay made and not the catalog's own answer.

An overlay supplied as a whole GovernedEntry keeps its own provenance: a LOCAL- entry id that could never be mistaken for an NDS- catalog row, its own confidence below 1.0, its own kind and its own candidate set.

An overlay for a token the catalog has never heard of. Without it KYC is a passthrough; with it the token is known, and this is the route by which a caller fixes an unknown without waiting for a catalog change.
allow_override=false demotes an overlay that CONTRADICTS the catalog. The governed answer stands, the source reverts to pinned, and the overlay's entry_id is nowhere in the record.
The demotion applies to whole-entry overlays as well as bare strings. The overlay pins DEP back to the catalog-wide Department; the domain pin refuses it and the LOCAL- provenance does not survive.

The distinction the contract calls out. An overlay for a token the catalog does not know is applied even under allow_override=false, because overriding nothing is not an override - and refusing it would leave the caller with an unknown token and no way to fix it.
An overlay that mentions a different token changes nothing about this one. The demotion is per token, not a switch that turns the whole overlay off.
Layers compose and the last one wins. Both layers define KYC with different long forms, so the answer says which layering order was applied.
The same two layers in the opposite order give the other answer. That is what distinguishes composition from a set union, which would have no order to disagree about.
Layering replaces a whole entry rather than merging it field by field: the later layer's canonical, entry id and confidence all arrive together.
Reversing the layers gives the other entry whole - the 0.9 confidence proves no field of the winning layer leaked from the losing one.
The first layer says nothing about TXN, so the catalog answers.
A later layer may introduce an override the earlier one never mentioned, so layering adds decisions rather than only replacing them.
A call-scoped custom= argument layers on top of an overlay the dictionary already carries, and wins. The dictionary itself is untouched; the layered copy is discarded when the call returns.

proves: An overlay applied across a whole identifier turns a partially unknown name into a fully known one, and the per-token provenance shows exactly which word the caller supplied and which three came from the catalog.

The overlay approves a token the catalog does not, and the finding says CUSTOM_ABBREV rather than APPROVED_ABBREV so a review can separate what the standard approved from what the caller did. ID is untouched by this overlay and still reports the catalog's own approval.

The house_style layer declares ID as well as WLT, and the overlay is consulted before the allow lists, so ID reports CUSTOM_ABBREV even though the catalog would have approved it anyway. The code names which authority actually fired, not the strongest one available.
The same name without the overlay fails, so the pass above is the overlay's doing and not a name that was compliant anyway.
The overlay is indexed in the reverse direction too, so a caller who declares a short form gets it both ways round - and the three-word phrase is matched as one unit by the longest-match scan.
With overrides allowed the overlay supplies the short form and the provenance says custom.

The demotion works in the reverse direction as well. The short form is the same either way, so the only thing that changes is the provenance - and it changes to the catalog row, which is the honest record of what decided it.
normalize leaves an overlay-approved token alone. It rewrites only what the vocabulary names an approved replacement for, and the overlay is the vocabulary saying WLT may stand.
